--- engine: knitr filters: - webr webr: show-startup-message: true cell-options: autorun: true --- # Design for Machining {#chap-machining} ## Learning Objectives {#sec-objectives-07} By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: 1. **Apply** Design for Machining (DFM) principles to reduce manufacturing costs 2. **Calculate** spindle speed and machining time for turning operations 3. **Identify** common design features that make parts difficult to machine 4. **Implement** guidelines for tolerances, hole sizes, and feature accessibility 5. **Evaluate** machining designs for automotive, food, and defense industry applications ::: {.callout-think} **Before You Read:** Why do you think DFM is particularly important in high-volume industries like automotive? Can you think of a part in your daily life that might have been designed poorly for machining? ::: ## Introduction to Design for Machining {#sec-machining-intro} Design for Machining (DFM) helps engineers create parts that are easy and cost-effective to machine. DFM principles reduce manufacturing costs, improve quality, and speed up production time. In this chapter, we'll explore the fundamentals of DFM, with real-world examples from the automotive, food, and defense industries. For a visual introduction to DFM in machining, check out these helpful YouTube videos: [Top Design Tips & Manufacturing Processes for Mechanical Engineers | DFM Guide](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sq3Ht-ivG5U) and [Only Real Mechanical Engineers Can Spot These Design Mistakes | CNC Machining](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rauL_J048sI).
--- ## DFM Guidelines for Machined Parts {#sec-machining-guidelines} Before diving into calculations, let's establish the fundamental design guidelines that make parts easier and cheaper to machine. ### Internal Corners and Fillets Sharp internal corners are impossible to machine with rotating cutters. Always specify **fillet radii** at internal corners. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Internal corners require fillet radii matching available tool sizes.](03-05-Machining_files/figure-html/fig-internal-corners-1.png){#fig-internal-corners fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: **Guideline:** Internal fillet radius should be at least **1.5× the tool radius** to allow the tool to move smoothly without dwelling in corners. ### Standard Hole Sizes Specifying standard drill sizes reduces tooling costs and setup time. | Preferred Hole Diameters (mm) | |:------------------------------| | 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 25, 28, 30 | ::: {.callout-check} **Quick Check:** A designer specifies a 7.3 mm diameter hole. Why might this cause problems in manufacturing? ::: ### Depth Limitations **Hole depth:** Standard drills can reliably produce holes up to **3× diameter** deep. Deeper holes require special tooling. **Pocket depth:** Avoid pockets deeper than **4× the tool diameter** to prevent tool deflection. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Hole and pocket depth guidelines relative to tool diameter.](03-05-Machining_files/figure-html/fig-depth-guidelines-1.png){#fig-depth-guidelines fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ### Wall Thickness Thin walls deflect under cutting forces, causing chatter and poor surface finish. Minimum wall thickness depends on material and wall height. | Material | Minimum Wall Thickness | |:---------|:-----------------------| | Steel | 3 mm or 0.1× height, whichever is greater | | Aluminum | 2 mm or 0.08× height | | Plastic | 1.5 mm | ::: {.callout-industry} **Automotive Application:** Engine block designers must balance thermal efficiency (thin walls for better cooling) against machinability (thick enough walls to resist cutting forces during cylinder boring). ::: --- ## Theory and Calculations {#sec-machining-theory} Design for Machining involves considering the capabilities and limitations of machining processes like milling, turning, and drilling during the design phase. Key principles include minimizing material removal, avoiding deep pockets, using standard hole sizes, and ensuring adequate tolerances. Mathematically, one core aspect is calculating spindle speed and feed rates to optimize machining. The spindle speed $N$ (in RPM) is given by: $$N = \frac{1000 \times v}{\pi \times D}$$ where $v$ is the cutting speed (m/min) and $D$ is the diameter being cut (mm): the **workpiece** diameter in turning, the **tool** diameter in milling and drilling. Machining time $T$ for a turning operation can be: $$T = \frac{L}{f \times N}$$ where $L$ is the length of cut (mm), and $f$ is the feed rate (mm/rev). Let's use R to perform a detailed example calculation. Suppose we're machining a shaft in the automotive industry with $v = 150$ m/min, $D = 20$ mm, $L = 100$ mm, and $f = 0.2$ mm/rev. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Define parameters v <- 150 ## cutting speed in m/min D <- 20 ## diameter in mm L <- 100 ## length in mm f <- 0.2 ## feed in mm/rev ## Calculate spindle speed N N <- (1000 * v) / (pi * D) N ## Calculate machining time T T <- L / (f * N) T ## in minutes ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2387.324 [1] 0.2094395 ``` ::: ::: This shows a spindle speed of approximately 2387.32 RPM and machining time of about 0.209 minutes. Now try other values yourself. Teaching demo --- drag the sliders and watch the spindle speed and the machining time respond. Which parameter changes the time the most? ```{=html}

Turning Time Calculator

Teaching demo
```
Show the live R code behind this calculator The card above re-runs this exact webR code every time you change an input. Edit the code directly and press **Run Code** to experiment further. ```{webr-r} #| label: machining-time-03-05 v <- 150 # cutting speed, m/min D <- 20 # workpiece diameter, mm L <- 100 # length of cut, mm f <- 0.2 # feed, mm/rev N <- (1000 * v) / (pi * D) # spindle speed, rev/min t_min <- L / (f * N) # machining time, min cat(sprintf("Machining time: %.3f min (%.1f s)\n", t_min, t_min * 60)) cat(sprintf(" Spindle speed N %.0f rev/min\n", N)) cat(sprintf(" Feed rate f * N %.0f mm/min\n", f * N)) ## Machining time against cutting speed for the current diameter, length and feed v_seq <- seq(50, 400, by = 5) t_seq <- L / (f * (1000 * v_seq) / (pi * D)) par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1)) plot(v_seq, t_seq, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue", log = "y", xlim = c(50, 400), ylim = c(0.005, 100), xlab = "Cutting speed (m/min)", ylab = "Machining time (min)", main = "Machining time vs cutting speed") points(v, t_min, pch = 19, cex = 1.8, col = "firebrick") ```
In industries like defense, where precision is critical, tolerances must be tight but achievable. Overly tight tolerances increase costs exponentially. ### Challenge Questions 1. Derive the formula for machining time if the feed rate changes with material hardness. 2. How would you adjust the cutting speed for a food industry application using stainless steel? ## Hands-on Examples Now, let's apply DFM to specific industries using R for analysis and visualization. ### Automotive Industry In automotive, DFM is used for engine components like pistons, camshafts and crankshafts. A plant turns a family of shafts with different diameters at the same cutting speed and feed. How does the turning time change with diameter? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Turning time for a family of automotive shafts of different diameter ## (same cutting speed, feed and length of cut as the example above) shafts <- data.frame(D = seq(10, 80, by = 5)) shafts$N <- 1000 * 150 / (pi * shafts$D) # spindle speed, rpm shafts$T <- 100 / (0.2 * shafts$N) # machining time, min ggplot(shafts, aes(x = D, y = T * 60)) + geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2) + geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 2.5) + theme_minimal() + labs(title = "Turning Time vs Shaft Diameter", subtitle = "v = 150 m/min, f = 0.2 mm/rev, L = 100 mm", x = "Shaft diameter D (mm)", y = "Machining time (s)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Horsepower vs Weight in Automotive Designs](03-05-Machining_files/figure-html/plot-auto-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: At constant cutting speed the spindle speed falls as $1/D$, so the turning time grows in proportion to the diameter. Doubling the shaft diameter doubles the time per pass. This is one reason designers keep turned diameters no larger than the function needs. ### Food Industry In the food industry, machined parts include conveyor rollers and mixing blades, often in food-grade stainless steel. Let's simulate data for machining costs vs. part complexity. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(42) complexity <- rnorm(50, mean = 5, sd = 2) cost <- 10 * complexity + rnorm(50, mean = 0, sd = 5) food_data <- data.frame(complexity, cost) ggplot(food_data, aes(x = complexity, y = cost)) + geom_point(color = "green") + geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, color = "darkgreen") + theme_minimal() + labs(title = "Machining Cost vs Part Complexity", x = "Complexity Score", y = "Cost ($)") + scale_color_viridis_d() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Simulated Machining Cost vs Complexity in Food Industry](03-05-Machining_files/figure-html/plot-food-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Higher complexity leads to higher costs—DFM aims to minimize this. ### Defense Industry For defense, parts like aircraft fittings require high precision. Let's create an interactive plot of how 100 simulated parts deviate from the nominal dimension, compared with a tolerance of $\pm 0.025$ mm. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Simulated deviation of 100 machined parts from the nominal dimension set.seed(123) deviation <- rnorm(100, mean = 0, sd = 0.01) defense_data <- data.frame(deviation) p <- ggplot(defense_data, aes(x = deviation)) + geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "firebrick", color = "black") + geom_vline(xintercept = c(-0.025, 0.025), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) + annotate("text", x = c(-0.025, 0.025), y = 13, label = c("LSL -0.025", "USL +0.025"), size = 3.5) + theme_minimal() + labs(title = "Machined Dimension: Deviation from Nominal", x = "Deviation from nominal (mm)", y = "Number of parts") if (knitr::is_html_output(excludes = "epub")) { plotly::ggplotly(p) } else { p } ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: This interactive histogram allows you to hover over bins to see details. The process spread (standard deviation 0.01 mm) fits inside the $\pm 0.025$ mm limits, but a few parts land close to them. A tighter tolerance would need a more capable (and more expensive) process. ### Challenge Questions 1. Modify the automotive plot for aluminum shafts cut at 400 m/min. How much shorter is the turning time? 2. In the food industry simulation, add a variable for material type and replot. How does it affect costs? 3. For the defense plot, change the standard deviation to 0.005. How does a more capable process change the number of parts near the tolerance limits? ## Interactive Exercises Try modifying the R code chunks above! For example, change the parameters in the machining calculation and rerun. Think critically: How would DFM principles alter a design with sharp internal corners in an automotive bracket? --- ## Tolerance and Surface Finish {#sec-machining-tolerances} Tolerances and surface finish specifications have a dramatic impact on machining cost. The relationship is exponential, not linear. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Relative machining cost increases exponentially as tolerances tighten.](03-05-Machining_files/figure-html/fig-tolerance-cost-1.png){#fig-tolerance-cost fig-align='center' width=864} ::: ::: **Design Guideline:** Only specify tight tolerances where functionally necessary. A ±0.1 mm tolerance costs approximately 2.5× more than ±0.5 mm, while ±0.01 mm costs 15× more. ::: {.callout-discussion} **Group Discussion:** Review a mechanical assembly drawing. Identify which dimensions truly require tight tolerances (fits, sealing surfaces) and which could be relaxed without affecting function. ::: --- ## Common DFM Mistakes to Avoid {#sec-machining-mistakes} | Mistake | Problem | Solution | |:--------|:--------|:---------| | Sharp internal corners | Tool cannot reach; requires EDM | Add fillet radius ≥ tool radius | | Non-standard hole sizes | Requires custom drills; added setup | Use standard drill sizes | | Deep narrow pockets | Tool deflection; poor finish | Limit depth to 4× tool diameter | | Unnecessary tight tolerances | Exponential cost increase | Tolerance only critical features | | Thin walls | Chatter; deflection | Maintain minimum wall thickness | | Blind holes with flat bottoms | Standard drills leave points | Accept drill point or specify boring | | Features on multiple sides | Multiple setups required | Consolidate features to fewer sides | ::: {.callout-think} **Design Challenge:** You have a bracket that requires holes on three different faces. How could you redesign it to reduce the number of machining setups? ::: --- ## Try it yourself {#sec-machining-tryit} ### Spindle speed and turning time {#sec-tryit-spindle} A carbide tool turns a $32$ mm diameter steel shaft over a length of $240$ mm at a cutting speed of $180$ m/min with a feed of $0.25$ mm/rev. The same shaft in stainless steel is cut at $70$ m/min. ```{=html}
```
Show the worked solution $N = \dfrac{1000 \times 180}{\pi \times 32} = 1790$ rpm and $T = \dfrac{240}{0.25 \times 1790} = 0.54$ min ($32$ s). For stainless at 70 m/min: $N = 696$ rpm and $T = 1.38$ min, about 2.6 times as long.
### What does the tolerance cost? {#sec-tryit-tolerance-cost} Use the chapter's cost curve: relative cost 1 at $\pm 0.5$ mm, 1.5 at $\pm 0.25$, 2.5 at $\pm 0.1$, 4 at $\pm 0.05$, 7 at $\pm 0.025$, 15 at $\pm 0.01$ and 30 at $\pm 0.005$. A feature machined at $\pm 0.5$ mm costs \$12. ```{=html}
```
Show the worked solution ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} | Feature | Tolerance (mm) | Relative cost | Cost ($) | |:-----------------:|:--------------:|:-------------:|:--------:| | Bearing bore | 0.025 | 7.0 | 84 | | Mounting face | 0.250 | 1.5 | 18 | | Slot width | 0.100 | 2.5 | 30 | | Locating pin hole | 0.010 | 15.0 | 180 | | Cover recess | 0.500 | 1.0 | 12 | ::: ::: Total \$324. Of that, the locating pin hole alone costs \$180 (56%). Relaxing the three non-critical features saves only \$24, but relaxing the pin hole to $\pm 0.05$ mm brings the part to \$168: attack the tightest tolerance first.
### Can the cutter make that corner? {#sec-tryit-corners} An end mill can only produce an internal corner radius of at least half its diameter. ```{=html}
``` ## Check Your Understanding ::: {.question} **Question 1:** What is the formula for spindle speed? a) $N = \frac{\pi D}{1000 v}$ b) $N = \frac{1000 v}{\pi D}$ c) $N = \pi D v$ ::: ::: {.answer} **Answer: b** The spindle speed formula is $N = \frac{1000 v}{\pi D}$ where $v$ is cutting speed in m/min and $D$ is diameter in mm. ::: ::: {.question} **Question 2:** In which industry might hygiene requirements most affect material choice for machining? a) Automotive b) Food c) Defense ::: ::: {.answer} **Answer: b) Food** Food processing equipment must use materials like 316 stainless steel that resist corrosion, can be sanitized, and won't contaminate products. ::: ::: {.question} **Question 3:** True or False: Tighter tolerances always reduce manufacturing costs. ::: ::: {.answer} **Answer: False** Tighter tolerances dramatically *increase* manufacturing costs. On the chapter's cost curve, each tenfold tightening of the tolerance multiplies the cost by about 4 to 8. ::: --- ## Practice Problems {#sec-machining-practice} ::: {.question} **Problem 1:** Calculate the spindle speed and machining time for turning a 50 mm diameter shaft, 200 mm long. The material is aluminum with a recommended cutting speed of 300 m/min. Use a feed rate of 0.3 mm/rev. ::: ::: {.answer} **Solution:** **Spindle Speed:** $$N = \frac{1000 \times v}{\pi \times D} = \frac{1000 \times 300}{\pi \times 50} = \frac{300000}{157.08} = 1910 \text{ RPM}$$ **Machining Time:** $$T = \frac{L}{f \times N} = \frac{200}{0.3 \times 1910} = \frac{200}{573} = 0.35 \text{ minutes} = 21 \text{ seconds}$$ ::: ::: {.question} **Problem 2:** A designer specifies internal corners with 1 mm fillet radius in a pocket. The smallest available end mill has an 8 mm diameter (4 mm radius). Will this design work? What should the designer change? ::: ::: {.answer} **Solution:** No, this design will not work. The 8 mm end mill has a 4 mm radius, so the minimum internal fillet it can produce is 4 mm—not 1 mm. **Recommendations:** 1. Increase the internal fillet radius to at least 4 mm (preferably 6 mm for smoother tool motion) 2. Or, specify that corners be finished with EDM (electrical discharge machining) at significant additional cost 3. Or, redesign to eliminate the pocket entirely ::: ::: {.question} **Problem 3:** A part requires the following tolerances. Estimate the relative machining cost if the baseline (±0.5 mm) costs $10 per part. - Feature A: ±0.5 mm - Feature B: ±0.1 mm - Feature C: ±0.025 mm ::: ::: {.answer} **Solution:** Using the tolerance-cost relationship: - Feature A (±0.5 mm): 1× baseline = $10 - Feature B (±0.1 mm): ~2.5× baseline = $25 - Feature C (±0.025 mm): ~7× baseline = $70 **Total estimated machining cost: $105 per part** Note: If Feature C could be relaxed to ±0.1 mm, the total would drop to $60—a 43% cost reduction. ::: --- ## Key Takeaways {#sec-machining-takeaways} 1. **Design with standard tools in mind:** Use standard drill sizes, avoid sharp internal corners, and limit feature depths to standard tool capabilities. 2. **Tolerances drive cost:** The relationship between tolerance and cost is exponential. Only specify tight tolerances where functionally necessary. 3. **Minimize setups:** Design parts so all features can be machined from as few orientations as possible. Each setup adds time and potential alignment error. 4. **Understand spindle speed and feed:** The formulas $N = \frac{1000v}{\pi D}$ and $T = \frac{L}{fN}$ are fundamental to predicting machining time and cost. 5. **Material matters:** Material selection affects cutting speeds, tool wear, and achievable tolerances. Harder materials require slower speeds and cost more to machine. --- ## Further Resources {#sec-machining-resources} **Videos:**
